# Service and compatibility design

The standalone app declares `eu.darken.porter.permission.API_V23`. Its manager-only permission is `eu.darken.porter.permission.MANAGER`. It does not declare or request the legacy API permission.

Porter sends binders to `${clientPackage}.porter` for clients requesting its permission. It sends to `${clientPackage}.shizuku` for legacy-only clients only when the optional companion owns the legacy permission and has the same signing certificate as Porter. The signature and permission declaration are checked in user 0 because permission ownership is device-global. Other manager apps are excluded from client delivery.

The client adapter retains the existing Shizuku SDK and wire protocol. Two provider classes gate incoming connections using a backend selected once per client process. AUTO prefers installed Porter, otherwise Shizuku. An explicit selection is persisted for the next process. This avoids switching a live SDK singleton while user services and permission callbacks are active. The original `.shizuku` authority remains available for the SDK's intra-app multiprocess binder lookup.

The manager receives its binder and user-service attachment requests through `eu.darken.porter.porter`. The companion holds no binder and exposes no provider: the SDK only calls a `.shizuku` `getBinder` inside the same application, so a companion-side bridge would have no legitimate caller and would hand the service binder to any app. All privileged operations still require the original caller's authorization at the service. The companion launcher opens Porter and its terminal receiver targets Porter explicitly.

`porter_server` and `/data/user_de/0/com.android.shell/porter.json` are independent of the original service's process and state. Shell-mode services still share Android's shell UID; separate app identities are not an operating-system security boundary between privileged services.

Porter's persisted decisions are authoritative. Grants from another manager are not imported. Runtime permissions are synchronized for clients that request them; the legacy permission is only touched while its owner is the trusted companion. If the mirrored primary runtime permission is missing when Android reports a permission change, the service starts, or a client attaches, the Porter grant is dropped and the client is prompted again on its next request. If the platform does not expose the permission-change listener, reconciliation falls back to startup and attachment. Decisions are saved synchronously to an atomic file owned by shell in both root and ADB modes. Users manage Porter authorization in Porter. Attaching to the service does not require a declared client permission: terminal clients started through rish fetch the binder themselves, are validated against their uid's packages, and appear in the management list once the user has decided on them. Compatibility is checked again for legacy delivery and unattached legacy calls so uninstalling the companion cannot enable a foreign manager's grants.

Do not rename AIDL descriptors, transaction codes, client callback semantics, parcelable class names, or Binder extra keys merely because they contain Shizuku's historical namespace. Application identity and wire-protocol identity serve different purposes.

Pre-v11 clients remain outside the upstream baseline's supported API range. A hardcoded package check is supported by the companion, but arbitrary explicit historical component names are not guaranteed aliases.
